title: Context Cloze
user: Independent language learners who know many word meanings but need to retrieve the right word in a sentence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN learner rejects flashcards in favor of open, sentence-completion questions because they prevent rote learning.
An Anki add-on proposal independently centers vocabulary review in meaningful sentences instead of isolated cards.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 language-learning discussions converge on the same failure: recognition cards do not exercise contextual recall; it directly affects daily study quality.
current_workaround: Learners hand-write cloze cards, search for example sentences, or use generic generated exercises.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki, Clozemaster, and Duolingo offer review or fixed curricula; none makes a learner-owned word list into a small, editable, context-first daily exercise without a gamified feed.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first web app that accepts a pasted word list and user-supplied example sentences, schedules typed cloze recall, and shows confusion pairs. Non-goals: dictionary licensing, AI chat tutoring, or a language course.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 50% of activated learners complete 12 sessions and add at least 30 personally chosen words.
monetization: one-time — personal vocabulary data should remain usable without an ongoing subscription.
constraints: Store lists locally by default; do not redistribute copyrighted example text; support Unicode and right-to-left scripts.
why_distinct: The unit of practice is productive sentence retrieval from a learner's own material, not another card deck or LLM wrapper.

title: Return Ramp
user: Self-learners with interrupted routines who need to restart a study habit without a punitive streak or a giant overdue queue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN explicitly debates a calm, non-gamified learning app and commenters object to distracting or coercive engagement mechanics.
An Anki user with difficulty maintaining habits says the current day-count experience is frustrating enough to consider quitting.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 discussions identify consistency friction and demotivating engagement design; the severity is abandonment of otherwise valuable study tools.
current_workaround: Reset a streak, lower new-card limits manually, skip backlog, or switch apps repeatedly.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo and many habit apps optimize streaks; Anki optimizes scheduling. Neither presents a deliberately low-pressure return plan that caps backlog and preserves continuity.
smallest_useful_product: An offline study-session planner with a missed-time check-in, a 5/10/20-minute return plan, backlog caps, and a private continuity calendar. Non-goals: social leaderboards, push-notification nagging, or replacing SRS algorithms.
success_measure: At least 40% of users who return after a seven-day gap complete three planned sessions in the following week.
monetization: free — trust depends on no engagement extraction; a paid export/theme option can be evaluated later.
constraints: No mental-health claims; all schedules and history must work offline and be exportable.
why_distinct: It treats restarting as the main job, rather than adding rewards to make a generic habit tracker stickier.

title: Reading Margin Recall
user: Language learners reading their own ebooks or web articles who need to turn selected passages into reviewable, source-linked notes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks for a language-learning tool combining ebooks, translations, and audiobooks; the response highlights synchronized reading features.
A learner says they could not find a simple, reliable way to capture interesting web content as Anki cards, so built an extension.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests show readers repeatedly bridge consumption and recall with brittle capture workflows.
current_workaround: Copy/paste into Anki, use a browser highlighter, or rely on a proprietary reader's word list.
incumbents_and_gap: Readlang, LingQ, Readwise, and Anki each cover part of the flow; the gap is a local, source-linked margin that produces recall prompts from user-owned text without hosting a content catalog.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension plus local PWA: highlight a sentence, add the user's gloss, choose a deletion, and review with a link back to the original page. Non-goals: OCR, ebook-store integration, automatic translation, or scraped libraries.
success_measure: At least 35% of activated users create 20 captures and review 10 of them on a later day.
monetization: one-time — private, personal reading metadata should not require an account.
constraints: Capture only user-selected text; do not fetch, republish, or bypass access controls for source content; keep data local.
why_distinct: The emphasis is transparent learner-authored retrieval from reading margins, not an AI summary or a replacement ebook reader.

title: Podcast Recall Loop
user: Self-learners who listen to educational podcasts and need to retain a handful of ideas without building a second knowledge-management system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN participants describe podcast listening as low-retention edutainment and resort to snippets, transcription, and Anki imports.
An Obsidian community project explicitly combines incremental reading, a reading queue, and flashcards, indicating continued demand for turning consumption into review.

recurrence: Two separate communities in 2025–26 describe the same consumption-to-retention gap; podcasts create a high-volume, low-recall failure mode.
current_workaround: Save timestamps in a podcast player, export highlights to Readwise, transcribe with AI, or abandon notes.
incumbents_and_gap: Snipd, Readwise, and podcast players capture highlights; full PKM systems are heavy. The missing product is a deliberately tiny recall loop from a manual timestamp to a later question.
smallest_useful_product: PWA with RSS episode lookup, manual timestamp clips, one learner-written takeaway/question per clip, and a three-question daily recall queue. Non-goals: transcription, copyrighted-audio hosting, auto-generated quizzes, or a social feed.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 30% of activated users create eight clips and answer at least half of their prompts seven days later.
monetization: one-time — it handles private notes and requires no server-side media processing.
constraints: Use podcast RSS metadata only; retain no audio; offer export as Markdown/CSV; preserve accessibility for keyboard use.
why_distinct: It deliberately limits capture to learner-authored recall prompts instead of becoming another transcript reader or AI note generator.

title: Self-Study Proofbook
user: Serious self-learners in math or CS who need a credible, private record of what they can actually solve rather than a course-completion badge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks how people validate deep self-study in math or CS; replies point to qualifying exams and independently solved problems.
A self-studier stresses needing texts with complete proofs, intuition, exercises, and no real-life help.

recurrence: Two independent self-study requests in 2025–26 expose a high-stakes evidence gap: work can be deep but difficult to assess or resume.
current_workaround: Keep a notebook, copy exam PDFs into a folder, post isolated questions online, or collect course certificates.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub portfolios show code and MOOCs show completion; neither creates a compact, source-cited ledger of attempted problems, timed attempts, revisions, and self-assessed evidence.
smallest_useful_product: Local Markdown-first proof/problem ledger with source citation, attempt timer, solution revision history, and printable mastery index. Non-goals: proctoring, grading claims, credential issuance, or answer generation.
success_measure: At least 25% of activated learners log 15 attempts across three topics and export one review sheet within 45 days.
monetization: one-time — the value is durable ownership of a learner's work archive.
constraints: Do not redistribute textbook or exam content; support local encrypted export; clearly state that records are not accredited credentials.
why_distinct: It records evidence of deliberate practice rather than pretending to certify knowledge or solve problems for the learner.

title: Prerequisite Pathboard
user: Adults relearning a technical subject who need to expose missing prerequisites and choose the next small concept deliberately.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN on relearning math includes an explicit approach of working backward through prerequisites from a concrete goal.
An Obsidian user reports that isolated cards worked for memory but lost the bigger conceptual picture and context.

recurrence: Two independent discussions point to the same structural issue: recall systems and resource lists do not reveal conceptual dependency or the next repair step.
current_workaround: Draw ad-hoc mind maps, follow a course sequence that does not match the goal, or accumulate disconnected notes/cards.
incumbents_and_gap: Obsidian graph view is unstructured; Khan Academy and MOOCs prescribe their own pathways. The gap is a learner-authored, goal-backward prerequisite board with evidence links.
smallest_useful_product: Offline graph board with goal nodes, prerequisite edges, a 'can explain/can solve/not yet' status, and one next-session recommendation derived only from user-entered dependencies. Non-goals: automatic curriculum generation, public content hosting, or mastery prediction.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilots add one goal with 12 nodes and complete five marked prerequisite repairs in a month.
monetization: one-time — learners need a long-lived, portable map rather than a course subscription.
constraints: All graph data exportable as JSON/Markdown; avoid claims of pedagogical diagnosis; accessible non-graph list view required.
why_distinct: It is a manual reasoning aid for dependency repair, not a prettier note graph or an LLM-created curriculum.

title: Explanation Lab
user: Students learning abstract STEM or programming concepts who need repeated practice explaining a mechanism, assumption, and counterexample in their own words.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks how people remember complex concepts and theories; a prominent response frames understanding as creating/building, not merely memorizing.
A coding tutor asks how to get grades 8–12 learners to use general reflective strategies for problem solving rather than only local fixes.

recurrence: Independent self-learners and tutors in 2025 ask for durable understanding and reflective transfer, a deeper problem than factual review.
current_workaround: Keep free-form notes, rubber-duck to a friend, answer forum posts, or ask an LLM to explain the idea back.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki measures recall and ChatGPT generates explanations; neither provides a constrained, reusable prompt sequence that makes a learner expose assumptions and test examples.
smallest_useful_product: Offline prompt cards for 'explain', 'draw a boundary', 'give an example', and 'find a counterexample', with dated self-recordings/text and a revisit queue. Non-goals: AI evaluation, plagiarism detection, grading, or a knowledge base.
success_measure: At least 40% of activated users complete 10 four-part explanations and revisit three after seven days.
monetization: free — a small privacy-respecting practice utility benefits from frictionless sharing by tutors.
constraints: Keep recordings local by default; transcription must be optional and on-device where supported; provide text-only use.
why_distinct: It makes explanation and counterexample generation a learner action, rather than outsourcing explanation to a chatbot.

title: Flex Practice Queue
user: Learners whose available study time arrives in short, irregular windows and who need to choose useful practice without breaking a formal scheduler.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN participants distinguish acquiring skill from remembering it and seek learning approaches beyond spaced repetition.
A Logseq learner explicitly wants to practice flashcards more than once per day but is blocked by the review workflow.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 threads show that a single daily SRS queue does not fit deliberate rehearsal, warm-up, or opportunistic five-minute study.
current_workaround: Reset cards, make duplicate decks, ignore a scheduler, or choose practice at random.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki and Logseq prioritize due reviews; generic to-do apps ignore retrieval. The gap is a separate, non-destructive practice queue that can mix weak items and voluntary drills.
smallest_useful_product: Offline queue builder that imports a CSV of prompts, lets users tag 'warm-up', 'weak', and 'today', runs timed mixed rounds, and never changes source-card scheduling. Non-goals: SRS replacement, shared decks, or automatic difficulty inference.
success_measure: Thirty percent of activated users run eight optional practice rounds in 21 days without modifying their primary card system.
monetization: one-time — import/export and local use are the core value.
constraints: CSV/Anki import must be read-only unless explicitly exported; retain no educational data remotely.
why_distinct: It adds an intentional rehearsal lane alongside scheduling rather than competing to be another flashcard scheduler.

title: Lesson Code Room
user: Teachers and tutors running live remote coding lessons who need one low-setup shared exercise space with visible learner progress.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Teachers/tutors report that remote coding lessons need zero install, zero account friction, few failure modes, and usable fallbacks.
A programming instructor seeks an online IDE for timed assignments and online sections, showing continued classroom demand for web-based execution.

recurrence: Two educator requests across 2025–26 identify setup friction and online exercise delivery as active teaching blockers.
current_workaround: Share Replit links, screen-share a local IDE, distribute files, or run separate video and coding tools.
incumbents_and_gap: Replit Classroom, GitHub Classroom, and CodeHS are broad platforms. The gap is a throwaway single-exercise room that opens without student accounts and gives a tutor only progress signals, not a full LMS.
smallest_useful_product: Hosted room with a teacher-created HTML/CSS/JS exercise, one join link, browser sandbox, run/reset, and anonymous progress states. Non-goals: Java/C++ execution, grading, proctoring, repositories, or video conferencing.
success_measure: A teacher can launch a room to 10 learners in under five minutes, and 80% run the starter exercise within two minutes of joining.
monetization: freemium — free small rooms validate adoption; paid plans cover concurrent sandbox sessions for tutors.
constraints: Strict iframe/CSP sandboxing, short retention, no student PII requirement, accessibility, and clear limits against using it for surveillance.
why_distinct: It intentionally solves the first ten minutes of a live lesson instead of recreating an IDE, LMS, or monitoring product.

title: Kid Code Missions
user: Parents and tutors introducing ages 7–13 to programming who need short, interest-led missions that teach sequencing and debugging before syntax-heavy courses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks how to teach a four-year-old to code; responses favor Logo, ScratchJr, games, and concrete playful activities.
A tutor describes a seventh-grader who wants Python and whose parents want it connected to AI, illustrating the need to set an age-appropriate learning path.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 educator/parent contexts show recurring demand for a bridge from child curiosity to real programming concepts.
current_workaround: Start with Scratch, YouTube tutorials, worksheets, or prematurely jump into Python/AI tools.
incumbents_and_gap: ScratchJr and Scratch are strong creative environments; coding-course subscriptions are curricular. The gap is a facilitator-friendly set of 10-minute unplugged-to-screen missions that explicitly rehearse debugging and instructions.
smallest_useful_product: Printable/PWA mission deck with one household-object challenge, one tiny browser simulation, and a parent prompt per mission; progress is local stickers only. Non-goals: chatbots, code generation, online communities, or a full coding curriculum.
success_measure: In parent testing, 60% of families complete four missions in two weeks and the child can verbally identify one debugging step.
monetization: one-time — a finite, printable family kit is clearer and less exploitative than recurring child engagement billing.
constraints: COPPA-conscious: no child accounts, analytics, chat, or public sharing; use original art/content and provide printable accessibility guidance.
why_distinct: It is a compact facilitation tool for computational habits, not a clone of a block-programming environment or an AI coding tutor.

title: Trace Before Run
user: Beginning programming students who can write fragments of Python but struggle to apply logic and debug simple problems.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN discussion about introducing a 13-year-old to programming emphasizes logic, branching, loops, decomposition, debugging, and self-correction before language preference.
A Python learner directly reports difficulty applying logical thinking to basic exercises and homework.

recurrence: A learner and an independent parent/educator discussion in 2025 point to the same early-stage transfer problem: syntax exposure does not create tracing or decomposition habits.
current_workaround: Watch tutorials, ask an LLM for the answer, repeatedly run code, or copy solutions from practice sites.
incumbents_and_gap: Python Tutor visualizes executions and coding platforms grade answers; the unresolved gap is a quick prediction-first drill where learners commit to a trace before seeing output.
smallest_useful_product: Static browser game with short editable Python-like snippets, variable-table prediction, branch-path selection, reveal-after-commit, and original micro-puzzles. Non-goals: code execution for arbitrary input, accounts, ranking, or an AI hint bot.
success_measure: After five sessions, 60% of test learners improve at least 20 percentage points on an unseen five-item trace quiz.
monetization: free — an open, linkable drill works best for teachers assigning it without procurement.
constraints: Use a restricted hand-authored grammar rather than executing user code; meet keyboard and color-contrast requirements.
why_distinct: Prediction before execution is the product mechanic; it is neither a generic code playground nor an answer-generating tutor.

title: In-Class Draft Ticket
user: Writing teachers who need a humane way to document authentic in-class drafting after AI has made take-home written work hard to assess.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks why AI has not eliminated graded homework; replies say there is no scalable alternative and classes are shifting work toward in-person explanation.
A writing teacher reports shifting to in-class writing because of LLM use and asks about the practical drawbacks of lockdown-browser drafts.

recurrence: Two 2025 educator discussions show assessment authenticity is urgent, while invasive lockdown and surveillance approaches are undesirable or impractical.
current_workaround: Handwritten drafts, LockDown Browser, oral defenses, Google Docs history, or more proctored exams.
incumbents_and_gap: LockDown Browser restricts devices and AI detectors make unreliable claims. The gap is a teacher-controlled, privacy-minimal record of process checkpoints rather than a system that tries to detect authorship.
smallest_useful_product: Teacher PWA generates a session code and a short draft ticket: claim, evidence location, revision choice, and exit reflection; students submit pseudonymous tickets and the teacher exports a session sheet. Non-goals: AI detection, webcam proctoring, keystroke logging, or blocking other software.
success_measure: In a five-class pilot, 80% of students complete a ticket in under three minutes and the teacher reports it informs feedback for at least half the drafts.
monetization: freemium — individual teachers need a free small-class tier; paid plans can fund encrypted class storage and exports.
constraints: FERPA/GDPR-conscious data minimization, no biometric or behavioral surveillance, short configurable retention, accessibility, and no claim of proving authorship.
why_distinct: It makes a lightweight pedagogical process artifact rather than policing students with AI detection or lockdown controls.
